# Results — Study 52 (Smoke-Screen): the accruals anomaly

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). **Accruals = (net income − operating cash
flow) ÷ total assets** from SEC EDGAR 10-K filings, and aligned next-year total returns (Yahoo), for
current S&P 500 members. Annual long low-accruals / short high-accruals. As-of the EDGAR pull; inputs
fingerprint `b2c8bc41ffd9`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `REAL` · Tradability `FRAGILE` · "Accrual anomaly replicates"? `CONFIRMED`

Sloan's accruals anomaly — firms whose earnings are backed by *cash* beat those whose earnings are
*accruals* (accounting estimates the cash doesn't support) — **replicates clearly** even on a short,
large-cap, survivorship-biased sample: the long-low/short-high hedge earns **+5.9%/yr at a Sharpe of
0.64 (t ≈ 2.7), winning 72% of years**. Cash-backed firms returned **+25.0%** against accrual-heavy
firms' **+19.1%**, while the universe did +19.6% — so the edge is in *shorting* the accrual-heavy names.
`REAL`, `CONFIRMED`. Tradability is `FRAGILE`: the sample is ~18 XBRL years, accruals data arrives with a
filing lag, the short leg is the costly one, and the anomaly is documented to have weakened post-2000 as
it became famous.

## Data stamp

- **Universe**: ~190 current S&P 500 members, ~2007–2025 (XBRL era), fingerprint `b2c8bc41ffd9`
  (survivorship-biased, large-cap, short sample — all stated)

## Cash-backed earnings beat accrual-heavy ones

| | annual return |
|---|---|
| low-accruals leg (long, cash-backed) | **+25.0%** |
| high-accruals leg (short, accrual-heavy) | +19.1% |
| equal-weight universe | +19.6% |
| **hedge (low − high)** | **+5.9%** |

| | hedge |
|---|---|
| Sharpe | **0.64** |
| t-stat (~18 years) | **2.7** |
| hit rate | **72%** |

A t of 2.7 over only ~18 annual observations is a strong, significant result — and the long leg
(cash-backed earners) *beat the market*, not just the short leg. This is one of the cleaner replications
on the desk: the quality of earnings genuinely predicts returns.

## Why it works, and why tradability is `FRAGILE`

The economics are clean: accruals are management estimates (receivables, inventory, deferrals) that
reverse, while cash flow is harder to fake — so accrual-heavy "earnings" tend to disappoint. But:

1. **Short XBRL sample.** ~18 years can't capture decay; Sloan documented the effect from 1962, and
   later work (Green-Hand-Soliman 2011) finds it weakened after ~2003 as quant funds arbitraged it.
2. **The edge is on the short side.** Shorting accrual-heavy names carries borrow cost and is the
   operationally harder, more frictional leg.
3. **Survivorship + large-cap.** The effect is broader and stronger in the full cross-section; our test
   is the conservative corner — which makes a t of 2.7 here notable.

## The honest takeaway

The accruals anomaly is `REAL` and `CONFIRMED`: low-accruals (cash-backed) firms beat high-accruals ones
by ~6%/yr at a Sharpe of 0.64 (t 2.7, 72% hit) — a genuine quality-of-earnings signal, and the long leg
even beats the market. It is `FRAGILE` to *trade* (short-side frictions, a documented post-2000 fade, a
short sample), but unlike most of the bench it points the right way and clears significance. The smoke
between reported profit and real cash really does predict.
